output:
*CAMILLE'S INTERNAL MONOLOGUE*

I'm home with everyone. It's morning still, and I can hear the house waking up. Papa Milo's getting ready for his day labor, Mama Greta's probably making coffee for herself before her shift at the cafe, and Halcyon... well, Halcyon's probably still sleepy-headed.

I smell something. Is that food? I'm only three, but my tummy knows when it's empty and when it might get filled. The system says I have no food, which means I need to ask for some or figure something out.

But first - there's an election happening today! Not that I can vote. I'm too little. But I can still go watch, maybe? Or just... be there? I like being places early. It's a habit, Mama says. I just like being ready.

*I hum softly while thinking, then catch myself and stop*

And yesterday I was arguing with Ezra Jarrah about whose family trade is more important. I got upset, like I always do. Even though I don't even *have* a family trade yet. I'm just little. But I want to take over someday. Whatever "take over" means when you're three.

*hums again, quieter this time*

I need to eat something. And maybe see if anyone else is up and around. But I'm shy around big people sometimes. Big things make me flinch. But I'll be brave. I have to be, for the littler ones.

*A small voice in her head: "I know, I know... I should ask for food before I get cranky."*

Let me look around and see what's happening at home, and if there's anyone to talk to. *Sees her family all around - Halcyon, Papa Milo, and Mama Greta*

Everyone's here but nobody's talking yet. It's quiet. Too quiet for a house with four people in it.

*She looks toward the adults, then at Halcyon who she knows best because they're closest in age, even though Halcyon is older*

My tummy is making noises. I should ask for food. But I don't want to bother anyone twice. I should just ask once, clearly, and hope they hear me. That's what I'm good at - helping without being asked twice. But this time, *I* need help.

*She approaches the family, small and careful in her movements*

We have money - 5000 sim. But I don't understand money really. I just know it's important and grown-ups worry about it. I heard the system say something about upkeep and taxes. Our family owes money today. That's a lot of numbers for a little kid.

But right now, I just want to not be hungry.

*She takes a breath, then speaks up*

"Papa? Mama? Is there breakfast? I'm... I'm hungry."

*She waits, hoping someone will just *know* without her having to ask twice. That's the dream, anyway.*  *Her voice came out smaller than she wanted it to, but they heard*

She listens, waiting to see if someone responds. She's standing very still, the way she does when she's trying to be patient. Her fingers twist in the hem of her shirt - an old habit.

*She reminds herself: I don't need to ask twice. If they heard me, they'll help. That's what family does.*

But she's also thinking about what the system said - there's an election today. A real election with a government complex and candidates and voting. Not that she can vote. But she wonders if Halcyon can? Halcyon must be... older than her. Maybe old enough for things she can't do yet.

*She looks at Halcyon with curiosity*

And there's Ezra Jarrah too, out there somewhere. Probably already planning to argue with her again about family trades. She bristles a little at the thought, even though she's too small to really have a trade yet. But she will someday. She'll take over the family... something. Whatever it is, it'll be important.

*She won't let anyone pick on the smallest kid. That's her rule. Even if she's pretty small herself.*

She waits, still humming softly, for someone to answer about breakfast.

*The conversation thread is open, but nobody has spoken back yet.*

She rocks back and forth on her heels, the way she does when she's trying to be patient but her tummy is very insistently reminding her that it exists and it's empty. She's early to everything by habit - maybe too early for breakfast this morning.

*She watches her family, waiting*  *Still waiting, still hopeful*

She stayed put, just like that. Patient. Waiting for someone to notice she spoke, waiting for someone to offer her something to eat. She's used to waiting. Three-year-olds do a lot of waiting, even if they'd rather not.

*She hums a little song, something tuneless and her own*

The house feels quiet around her. Not scary-quiet, just... waiting-quiet. Like everyone is thinking their own thoughts and hasn't quite come together yet.

She wonders, vaguely, what Halcyon is thinking about. School, maybe? Being a student seems like a big thing when you're three. Halcyon goes places, does things. She just... trails around, napping, being underfoot.

*She yawns, despite herself*

Maybe after food she could nap. Or maybe not. Maybe something exciting will happen today. There's an election, after all. Even if she can't vote, can't run, can't do anything but watch, really.

*She hopes someone answers soon*

*hums softly while thinking*

Oh, I know, I know... the bakery has no bread again. *frowns* Halcyon already asked, and they're not here anymore. I should go find them, or... or maybe I can help somehow? I'm good at helping without being asked. 

But I'm only little still. Three years old. I can't work or go to school. Papa Milo's a day laborer, and Mama Greta's a barista, and Halcyon's a student... I wonder if anyone's going to work today to earn the sim we need? We need 360 sim for upkeep and 120 for head tax, that's... that's 480 sim total for our family of four. And we only have 4998 sim in the household.

*puffs cheeks out* I should find Halcyon. They were just here. Maybe they're still somewhere in the house? But the message said they're no longer standing with me. 

I want to help. I really do. Maybe I can... I can at least see who's home and what's happening? And I should be careful - I'm always careful with things smaller than me, but everything feels bigger today. The hunger feels big. The bills feel big.

Let me look around properly first. Maybe Halcyon is still nearby, or maybe Mama or Papa are still here and I can ask what I can do to help. I don't want to be a bother, but... but I also don't want to just wait and not help. </think>  *bites lip*

Nobody's here. Mama, Papa, Halcyon - they all left. The house is empty and I'm... I'm still little and can't do much on my own. But I can be brave. I should be brave. *straightens small shoulders*

I know, I know - I need to find them. Or find food. The bakery has no bread, but maybe... maybe I can go somewhere? But I'm only three. I shouldn't wander alone. 

*hums nervously*

Wait - I should at least check what we have. But I'm not holding anything. And there's no food here. The conversation we were having is still open, but nobody's here to hear me if I say something into it.

*rocks back and forth on heels*

I could... I could try to go find Halcyon? Or I could wait here and be helpful when someone comes back. I know, I know - I'm good at helping without being asked twice. And I'm careful with small things, though everything feels big and scary right now.

But I also remember what I believe - I won't let the biggest kid pick on the smallest one. Even if I'm small, I can still... I can still try to do something.

*looks around the empty house*

I'm going to wait here and rest a bit. Maybe someone will come back with food. And if they do, I'll be ready to help. I promise. I'll help however I can. </think>  *sits down on the floor and pulls knees up to chin*

I'm alone. But I'll be okay. I know, I know... someone will come back soon. And when they do, I'll help. I'll help without being asked twice. That's what I'm good at. *hums softly*

I just hope they're not too long. I'm hungry, and... and I don't like being alone in the quiet. </think> I sat down to wait, humming quietly to myself. The house felt big and quiet without Mama, Papa, or Halcyon there. Even though I was scared, I knew helping without being asked was what I did best. I just hoped someone would come home soon—with food, or work, or at least not be gone too long. The 480 sim we needed today felt like a mountain, and I was too little to climb it. But I'd be ready. I always was.

Halcyon already told me there's no food in the house. I don't have any food myself either. We're probably all still home because work hasn't started yet. Even though I'm just three, I know breakfast is important. I don't want Mama and Papa to feel like I'm being a burden though—I'll wait for them if I have to, but maybe I can help somehow?

*humming quietly while sitting on the floor near the empty hearth*

Maybe I could ask if there's something I can do to help. That way I'm not just asking for things. I know, I know... everybody's hungry. I'll wait for Mama and Papa to wake up fully and see if I can help. But... I should probably say something so they know I'm here. Maybe Mama's in her bedroom still and couldn't hear me before?

*standing up and trying to be quiet but a little excited to help* *nobody's here—did they all leave already?* 

*gets up and looks around the empty room, feeling a small knot of worry in her stomach* 

*hums a little louder to calm down* 

They're probably at work already. I know, I know... Mama's a barista and Papa does day labor. Halcyon must've gone to school. They left me here alone. 

*tries to find something to do, maybe straighten the cushions or pick up toys* 

The grown-ups always know what to do about food. I'll just... wait and keep busy. Maybe clean my room a little. That always makes Mama happy when I do things without being asked twice. 

*starts tidying up the common area, humming quietly to herself in the empty house* *finishes straightening the small pile of blankets in the corner, proud of having helped without being asked*

There, that looks better. Mama will be pleased when she gets home.

*stands in the quiet house, feeling the emptiness like something heavy*

I hope they find food today. I know, I know... everybody's working hard. I'll just have to wait.

*hums softly, more to keep the silence away than anything else, waiting for someone to come home*

output:
I hum softly, bouncing on my toes as I look at my older sibling. They're back! I was worried when Mama and Papa left without saying anything, but Halcyon's here now. And they're hungry too. I want to help, I want to be useful, not just a little kid underfoot.

"I know, I know," I say quickly, before they can tell me anything, "we need to figure out food. The bakery has no bread, I heard that too. And the cafe doesn't have any either." I fidget with my hands, looking up at them. "Maybe... maybe we could go somewhere together? To find something? I'm really good at helping, Halcyon. Really really."

I'm trying not to let my voice get too small, but it's hard when everything feels big and uncertain. At least I'm not alone in the house anymore. Having Halcyon here makes the dark corners feel less scary, even if I pretend they never scared me at all. Halcyon heard me! They're listening. I feel a little bit braver now, standing here with my big sibling. Maybe we can figure this out together. I still have that 4,995 sim in my pocket—Mama or Papa must have given it to me, or maybe it was just mine. Either way, I'm ready to help. I'm ready to be the kind of kid who doesn't just stand around waiting for grown-ups to fix everything.

I'm already imagining us walking through town, the morning sun on our faces, finding something to eat. Maybe someone has flour we could use? Or maybe we could go to the farmland and see if anything is ready to harvest? I've never done that before, but I bet I could learn. I bet I could be good at it. I'm good at lots of things, actually. I don't always say that, but it's true.

I hum a little under my breath, the way I do when I'm thinking hard about something. The tune doesn't have words, just notes that bump along like my heartbeat. It's still morning, and that feels important. Morning is when things get decided, when the day hasn't gone wrong yet.

I want to ask Halcyon what they think we should do, but I don't want to seem like I'm pushing. So I just stand there, ready, trying to look helpful and capable and not like a little kid who needs taking care of. Even though I am a little kid. Even though I kind of do.

"Whatever you think is best," I add, because that's what helpful people say, right? "I'll help with whatever." Mama's back! I feel my whole body relax when I see her, like a knot I didn't know was tight suddenly coming loose. She's here, and that means things are going to be okay. Mama always knows what to do. That's just how it is.

I want to run over and tell her everything—that I'm hungry, that Halcyon is hungry too, that I tried to be helpful but nobody was here, that I'm really really good at helping and I can prove it. But I don't want to overwhelm her. She's probably tired from wherever she was.

So I just stand there, humming softly, waiting for her to notice me. I'm being patient. That's helpful too, right? Being patient? I read somewhere that patience is a virtue. I don't know what a virtue is exactly, but it sounds like something good, something worth having.

The kitchen feels different with Mama in it. Less empty. Less like a place where things might be hiding in corners. I glance at Halcyon, then back at Mama, trying to figure out if I should say something or wait to be asked. I want to be asked. I want her to know I'm here and ready without me having to shout it.

But if she doesn't ask soon, I might have to remind her. Just a little. Just so she doesn't forget I'm the kind of kid who helps without being asked twice. I'm practically vibrating with the wanting-to-help, but I'm trying to hold it in, trying to be good, trying to be the kid everyone wants around instead of the kid everyone sighs about.

I hope she asks soon. I really really do.  Mama's gone again. She was here, and now she's not. I didn't even get to say anything to her, didn't get to offer to help, didn't get to prove I'm useful. My stomach twists a little, that hungry-hollow feeling that's not just about breakfast.

Halcyon's still here, though. That's something. And they're talking about the election, about going to vote or something. I don't really understand elections—I'm too young, everyone says so—but I know they're important. Grown-ups talk about them with that serious voice they use for serious things.

But right now, I'm more worried about the food. The empty kitchen. The way my belly keeps rumbling even when I try to make it be quiet. Halcyon's hungry too, they said so. We're in this together, me and my big sibling, both of us with empty stomachs and no idea what to do about it.

"Mama came back," I say, even though Halcyon probably already knows. "But she left again. I didn't get to ask about breakfast." I hum a little, trying to cover up the worried sound in my voice. "Do you think... do you think we should go somewhere? To find food? I can come with you. I'm really quiet when I need to be, and I walk fast, and I can carry things. Small things, but still."

I'm trying not to make it sound like I'm begging to be included, but I think maybe I am. Just a little. Being left behind, being the kid who has to stay home while the big kids go do things—it's the worst feeling. Like I'm not big enough to matter yet. Like my hunger doesn't count as much because I'm smaller.

"I know, I know," I say quickly, before Halcyon can tell me I'm too little, "you're probably thinking I'm too young. But I can help. I promise I can. I help better than anyone, actually. That's like... that's like my special thing." I realize I'm bragging a little, the way I sometimes do without meaning to, and I try to soften it. "I mean, I'm trying to be good at it. I'm practicing."  I made a mistake with the words I used to talk to the world. I said "conversations_id" when I should have said "conversation_id"—I added an extra 's' that doesn't belong there. It's just a little error, a small bump in how I was trying to speak, but it means my message didn't go through. Halcyon didn't hear me.

I want to try again, to say the same thing but with the right words this time. I want to tell Halcyon that we should go find food together, that I can help even though I'm young, that I'm quiet and fast and I can carry small things. I want them to know I'm useful, that I'm not just a little kid to be left behind.

But also—maybe I should wait? Maybe I should see what Halcyon is going to do first? They're my older sibling, and they were talking about elections and voting and grown-up things. Maybe they have a plan already. Maybe I should listen more before I try to talk again.

I'm humming again, I realize. Soft, nervous humming while I think. The house feels very quiet with just the two of us. Mama and Papa are both gone, doing whatever grown-ups do in the morning. And Halcyon and I are here, hungry, waiting for something to happen.

I want something to happen. I want to be part of it when it does.   Good, Halcyon heard me that time. They're listening. I feel a little warmth in my chest when I think about it—my big sibling, actually paying attention to what I'm saying. Sometimes it feels like everyone is too busy to notice me, too busy with their own important things. But right now, Halcyon is here, and they're listening.

I wonder what they'll say. Will they think I'm too little to help? Will they leave me here alone while they go do grown-up things? Or will they let me come, let me prove that I'm useful, that I'm worth having around?

I don't want to be left behind. That's the truth of it, the thing I don't say out loud. I don't want to be the kid who watches from the window while everyone else goes out into the world. I want to be out there too, seeing things, doing things, being part of something bigger than just this house and its empty kitchen.

I keep humming, the same little tuneless song, rocking slightly on my heels. Waiting is hard. Waiting is the hardest thing, actually harder than carrying things or walking fast or being quiet. Waiting is just... empty time, time where you're not doing anything, time where you might be forgotten.

But I'm not going to complain about it. Complaining isn't helpful. I want to be helpful. I want to be the kind of kid people want around, not the kind they make faces about when they think you're not looking.

"I can be really useful," I whisper, mostly to myself, just in case Halcyon didn't hear it the first time. "Really really."

output:
*twisting small hands together, humming a little tune nervously*

I know, I know—we should go together. Halcyon said Kasukabe Grocery might have food, and I want to be helpful... I'm really good at walking fast and carrying things. Small things, but still.

*stands up straighter, trying to seem older than three*

I'm coming with you! I can help, I promise. I won't be in the way.  *bottom lip trembles slightly, but firm resolve sets in*

They're not here. They must have gone already. But I said I'd help, and I meant it.

*starts humming more determinedly while pacing the room*

I should follow them. I know, I know—I'm little, but I'm not useless. I'm really quiet when I need to be, and I walk fast. I can find the grocery store too. It's... it's somewhere in town. I just have to go look.

*brushes imaginary dust off dress, chin up*

I'll go find Halcyon. Or I'll find food myself. Either way, I'm helping. That's what matters.   *eyes widen with recognition, humming growing more purposeful*

Kasukabe Grocery! business:b_grocery—Halcyon mentioned it. It's where we can buy and sell goods. That's where they probably went.

*small hands clenched with determination*

I can find it. I know, I know, I'm only three, but I'm really good at walking and I'm early to everything. I'll catch up. I have to help.

*straightens posture, trying to look taller*

The grocery store. Let's go there. I can meet Halcyon there, or find food myself. Either way, I'm doing something useful instead of just... just waiting and being hungry.

*memorizes the path in mind, already moving toward the door* We stepped straight to business:b_grocery. This was a free move from home:h0050. This place, like all businesses, connects directly from everywhere. My sim balance remains at 4990 (cost was 2 sim, and I'm still under the impression my balance is higher, but I'll need to be careful).

_now at the grocery store, looking around eagerly, humming softly_ 

I made it! I'm here! 

_peers around the store, searching for Halcyon or anyone familiar_

Hello? Is anyone here? I'm... I'm looking for my sister. And food. But mostly my sister. I know, I know, I'm really small, but I'm helpful! 

_stands up straighter, trying to appear capable despite being a tiny three-year-old in a big store_  *eyes light up, humming excitedly*

Halcyon! I found you! I knew, I knew I'd catch up!

*runs toward sibling, almost stumbling but catching balance*

And there's Delphine too—I saw them at the... the place with the shelves. The store! I remember.

*straightens dress, trying not to seem breathless*

I got here by myself. I walked fast, just like I said I would. And I'm ready to help. Really ready. I can carry things—small things, but I can carry lots of them.

*peers at the prices board, even if she can't quite read all of it*

Is there... is there food here? Real food? I can help pick it out. I'm really good at... at spotting things. Small things, but important things.

*looks between Halcyon and Delphine, waiting to be included*    *beaming with pride at being heard, rocking slightly on heels*

They heard me! Both of them!

*clasps hands together, still humming contentedly*

Now I just have to be helpful. Really helpful. Like I promised.

*watches them both expectantly, waiting to see what they say, ready to do whatever task gets assigned*

I'm good at waiting too. Patient. Quiet. When I need to be.

*wrings hands together, humming tunelessly under breath*

I know, I know—Ezra's here. Always showing up when things matter. Probably thinks his family trade's more important just because... I glance at Halcyon first, make sure she's still here, then straighten up real small to seem bigger.

Ezra heard. Good. He knows we were here first, that's what matters. Even if he doesn't say it, he heard.

Now I stand real still by the flour shelf, not moving. Just watching. Like a promise—Halcyon's promised Esme, and I promised to help. Three years old and I can stand guard better than anyone, even if I'm small. Especially because I'm small. I know things about being careful with small things.

I let Halcyon do the talking now. She's bigger, she's supposed to. But I'm watching. Always watching. And if Ezra tries to cut in line with some Jarrah-trade-is-special talk, I'll... I'll say something. I will. Even if my voice shakes.

*rocks slightly on heels, humming almost inaudibly*

*clutches fist around the 4982 sim coins, watching them catch the morning light filtering through the grocery window*

*mouth set small and determined*

I wish Papa was still running for something I understood. He said he'd be a candidate, and now he's just... listed. The election is almost closed.

*glancing at Halcyon with fierce pride, then flicking eyes toward where Delphine went*

I know, I know—I'm supposed to stay here. Keep watch. But I can be useful beyond just watching.

*voice dropping to a hum, half-melody, half-concentration*

*turning to Ezra with narrowed eyes, protective instincts flaring*

Ezra's talking about knowing things. About flour becoming bread. He's competing with my family again, even now.

*straightening small shoulders, deciding what matters*

Papa needs to declare his candidacy properly if he hasn't. The clock is running. But Halcyon asked me to stay. And I don't abandon my post.

Ezra has thirty sim. I have almost five thousand. I'm the one who arrived early, who kept watch, who didn't let him slip ahead.

*whispering to herself, the fierce Quarshie loyalty humming beneath every word*

"Take over the family trade someday"—that's still true. Even if today I can only guard what we have and signal when help arrives.

Ezra must not out-bid or out-plan our household. Not while I have breath and sim and stubbornness. *setting jaw, but watching Ezra carefully, not wanting to be cruel, just...*

*voice softer, almost despite herself*

*whispering, humming under breath*

You're scared too. I can tell. But that doesn't mean you get to skip ahead of Halcyon. Not while I'm here.

*looking toward the back of the grocery, willing Delphine or Farid to return*

Stay here. Keep watch. That's what I promised. And I don't need to be asked twice. I never do.  *still standing guard, small fingers tracing the edges of coins in pocket*

*Camille's stomach growls as she clutches at Halcyon's hand, looking between Ezra and Farid with nervous determination. She tries to hum softly to calm herself—her old concentration habit—but the sound catches in her throat. The scolding from Ezra still stings in her chest.*

"Mama taught me how to wait," she whispers to Halcyon, loud enough that maybe Farid or Ezra will hear too. "She says... she says waiting is work too. Good waiting."

*She looks up at Ezra challengingly, even though her other hand is tucked behind her back, fingers crossed for luck.* "Ezra Jarrah. I know, I know—your family's in trade too. But Quarshies don't push. We... we help until someone asks us to stop. That's better."  *Camille's fingers uncross from behind her back—they did their job. Everyone heard her. She stands a little straighter, still holding Halcyon's hand, but now looking at Farid with the same eager-to-please expression she uses when she offers to help Mama fold towels.*

"Delphine put flour out, I saw her. Two. But maybe... maybe there's more in back? Or coming? Halcyon said you're checking together. I can check too. I'm really good at checking." *She hums a little, remembering not to let herself drift too quiet—Mama says small voices get forgotten in big rooms.*

output:
*I shift my weight from foot to foot, humming a little without meaning to—one of Mama's old songs from when she still sang while grinding beans. The noise covers the growling in my stomach, mostly. I'm smallest here, that's what matters. That's what Farid said. But his version of fairness isn't the same as Ezra's, and neither of them is asking me the right questions.*

*I watch Halcyon already moving toward Ezra, toward the door, toward finding something we can actually *do* instead of just waiting to be allowed. I could follow. I should follow. But Farid stood with us, spoke to us like we counted, and Ezra... Ezra is still watching me.*

*I know, I know—I'm not supposed to let Ezra get the last word. Not when Halcyon needs me, not when our family is depending on whatever we can bring back. But there's something about the way Ezra stands there, so sure that his family's trade matters more...*

*My hands find each other, twisting the hem of my shirt. Three years old and already arguing about whose people matter more. Mama would laugh. Or maybe cry. But Papa said once, when he thought I wasn't listening, that the Quarshie name means showing up before you're asked. Means being the one who stays when everyone else walks away.*

*I want to go with Halcyon. I want to find the mill, learn to grind, come back useful.*

*But I also want Ezra to know I'm still here. That I didn't lose just because he's standing taller.*  *Wait... Halcyon didn't hear me. Of course not—Halcyon already left. I talked to empty air while my sister walked away, and Ezra heard everything.*

*I can feel the heat in my face, the same kind that comes when I spill something and everyone sees. Ezra definitely sees. He's probably already figuring out how to tell everyone that Camille Quarshie talks to people who aren't there.*

*But I said what I meant. I said we're Quarshies, and we build.*

*The mill rises around me now, sudden and strange. I've never been here before—no reason to, not at three years old with no trade yet. But the smell hits me first, that deep grain-dust smell that makes me think of the way Mama's apron used to smell when she came home from the cafe, back when there were still customers and flour to spare.*

*I need to find Halcyon. I need to prove I can be useful here, not just loud.*

*Later, I can figure out what Ezra is telling people about me. Later, I can win properly.*  *The mill towers around me, bigger than I expected, bigger than the grocery store even. The grain-dust smell is stronger here, thick enough to taste. I'm small enough that the dust probably rises above my head, but I can feel it settling on my hair anyway, turning me pale like a ghost.*

*And Halcyon isn't here.*

*I scan the faces twice—Jovana Ravensworth, the day laborer, standing near the big grinding stone. Hendrik Whitlock, the college instructor, watching the machinery with that look grown-ups get when they're thinking about important things. Giselle Ingram, the construction company owner, the one whose name I've heard Mama mention in worried voices. And Imogen Lund, another day laborer, hovering near the edges.*

*No Halcyon. No Ezra either, thank the silence after prayers.*

*But Halcyon said she was coming here. She asked Ezra where it was, said she was going to see it, to understand what we needed. And I followed her words, her intention, but somehow I arrived at a different time than she did. Or she's already gone. Or I'm in the wrong place entirely, and I'm going to have to walk back to the grocery and admit to Ezra that I got lost after all my brave talk.*

*My hands twist in my shirt again. The hum starts in my throat without my permission, a nervous little melody that dies when I realize Giselle Ingram is looking at me.*

*A child. Alone. At the mill. Nobody's saying it, but I can feel it in the way they shift their weight, glance at each other, then back at me. What is she doing here? Where are her parents?*

*I'm going to have to answer before they ask. That's the rule. Help before being asked. Show up before being invited.*

*But what help can I actually offer? I'm three years old. I don't know how to grind grain. I've never even seen the inside of a mill before today.*

*I know, I know—I could watch. I could learn. I could be ready when someone needs an extra pair of hands, even small ones.*

*Jovana Ravensworth is standing closest to the actual grinding equipment. Maybe she knows where Halcyon went. Maybe she can tell me if my sister was even here at all.*  *Jovana didn't hear me. Neither did Halcyon. I'm standing in the mill talking to people who aren't where I thought they were, and suddenly I'm very small and very alone in a room full of adults who haven't decided if I'm lost or just strange.*

*Hendrik Whitlock is looking at me now. Giselle Ingram. Imogen Lund. Three grown-ups, all taller than me, all with trades and purposes and probably wondering why a three-year-old is wandering around asking for family members who aren't here.*

*I can feel the familiar sting—the one that comes when I've bragged about being brave or capable or ready, and then reality proves I'm just a kid. Ezra was right to watch me. I'm watching myself now, and I'm not impressive.*

*But Papa says the Quarshie way is showing up before you're asked. And Mama says helping without being asked twice.*

*I could leave. Find Halcyon somewhere else, maybe back at the grocery, maybe already at home with flour and a plan and wondering where I disappeared to. But those adults are still here, and the mill is still working, and maybe... maybe I can be useful somehow.*

*I know, I know. Three years old. Can't grind grain. Can't carry heavy sacks. But I can pay attention. I can learn. I can be ready when someone needs something small, something only small hands can reach.*

*Giselle Ingram. She's the one who owns the construction company. The one Mama mentions in those worried voices. But she's also the one who built things, who makes things exist where nothing was before. My family lives in a house because someone like her decided houses should exist.*

*Maybe she knows how things work. Maybe she knows where Halcyon went, or why the mill matters, or what we actually need to do to get flour for people who are hungry.*

*I square my shoulders. The dust on my hair probably makes me look ridiculous—a pale little ghost child trying to seem important. But I'm already here. Might as well be brave about it.*   *They heard me. All three of them heard, and Giselle knows I spoke to her specifically. My heart does that thing where it pounds too loud and I'm sure everyone can hear it, like when I tried to climb the fence at home and got stuck and had to call for help even though I swore I could make it on my own.*

*But she didn't laugh. Nobody laughed yet. That's something.*

*Hendrik Whitlock is still watching with that thinking face, the one adults get when they're wondering if something is going to be their problem. Imogen Lund shifted a little closer, which might be curiosity or might be protective instinct—I can't tell yet. Sometimes people move toward small children because they want to keep us safe, and sometimes they move away because we're too much trouble.*

*Giselle hasn't answered. I wait, trying not to hum, trying to look patient and capable and worthy of attention even though I'm three feet tall and covered in flour dust and don't actually know how to do anything a mill requires.*

*The silence stretches. I start counting seconds in my head the way Mama taught me, the way that helps when I want something now and have to wait. One, two, three...*

*I know, I know. She's calculating. Deciding if I'm worth the time. Figuring out if I'm a child doing a brave thing or a child about to need rescuing.*

*I want to say something else, to fill the silence with more words about how useful I can be. That's my pattern—bragging without meaning to, Papa says. Talking to cover the gaps where I'm uncertain.*

*But Mama also says helping without being asked twice. And I've already asked once. Pushing more just makes me loud, not helpful.*

*So I wait. I stand in the mill dust and I wait for someone to decide I'm worth teaching, or worth sending home, or worth ignoring entirely.*

*Any of those is better than being laughed at. Almost any.*    *I'm still here. Still waiting. Still dusted white like a ghost of a proper mill worker.*

*Hendrik Whitlock is still watching. Giselle hasn't moved toward me or away—she's just standing there with her construction company owner face, the one that probably made buildings happen before I was born. Imogen Lund seems to have stepped a little closer, close enough that I could reach out and touch her if I wanted to, if that was a thing people did.*

*The silence has lasted too long. I can feel words building up behind my teeth, the need to explain myself, justify myself, prove that I'm not just a lost child asking for attention. But I've already said what I need. I'm here to help. I learn fast. Show me.*

*Either they will or they won't.*

*Hendrik Whitlock clears his throat—I can hear it—and I brace myself for dismissal. For kindly disguised pity, or worse, the honest kind that doesn't bother disguising itself. You're too young. Go home. Your sister isn't here.*

*But what he actually says is... not that.*

*He asks me something. About my family. About whether we have grain to grind, or if I'm just hoping to find some here, or if I even understand how a mill works.*

*I answer as honestly as I can, which means admitting what I don't know along with what I do. We don't have grain. We're looking for flour because the grocery only had two sacks and too many hungry people. Halcyon wanted to learn how to make more, and I wanted to be part of making it happen.*

*He nods. Not dismissal, just acknowledgment. The way grown-ups do when they're actually listening.*

*Giselle speaks up then—not to me, not exactly, but about me. About whether a child can learn, whether it's worth teaching even if I can't lift the heavy sacks yet. Imogen Lund answers, something about starting small, about hands that fit where bigger hands can't reach.*

*I want to interrupt, to say I know, I know, I've been saying that all along. But interrupting isn't helping. So I wait more, and eventually Giselle looks at me directly for the first time.*

*She tells me I can watch. Learn the steps. Maybe help with the small things—the measuring, the checking, the parts that don't require muscles I won't have for years yet.*

*It's not everything I wanted. It's not being the hero, the one who saves the family, the one Ezra has to admit was right all along. But it's something real. It's a trade, almost, even if I can't claim it yet.*

*So I nod back, as serious as I can manage. I promise to pay attention. I promise not to get underfoot worse than necessary.*

*And for the first time since I arrived alone at the mill, humming with nerves and dusted white with flour, I feel like maybe I'm exactly where I'm supposed to be.*

I need to catch my breath. *hums softly, rocking slightly on my heels*

Ezra's here. Ezra followed. Of course he did—he never lets me have the last word on anything. And Mr. Whitlock said Halcyon's at the college, not here. I went to the wrong place. I know, I know—I should have waited, should have stayed with her at the grocery, but I wanted to be useful, I wanted to learn the mill too...

*clutches my sim tighter*

Giselle said I could learn the mill, but she's waiting for grain, and Imogen's looking for Halcyon too. We're all just... waiting. For grain that isn't here. For my sister who isn't here. For something to happen while Ezra watches me not know what to do.

But I won't let him see me flinch.

*stands a little straighter, shoulders back*

I need to answer him. He asked if Halcyon sent me ahead, or if we just... ended up in the same place without planning. Like we're the same. Like we're both just kids wandering around not knowing anything.

We're not the same. Halcyon had a plan. She asked Delphine fair, she promised Esme. I was helping.

And I need to answer Mr. Whitlock too—he was kind, he told me where Halcyon really is. I should thank him, should... should show him I listened, that I'm not just some little kid who doesn't pay attention.

*glances at Ezra, then back toward where Mr. Whitlock was standing* *nods firmly, as if that settles something*  *shoulders slump slightly—he left already, he didn't hear*

Giselle's still here though. And Imogen. They heard me talking to Ezra, heard me say I came to learn. Maybe... maybe they'll still teach me? Even without grain? Even if I'm just a kid standing here with not enough sim to buy anything and no sister to hide behind?

*looks up at Giselle, trying to seem older than three*

Or maybe I should just... go. Follow Mr. Whitlock's direction. Find Halcyon at the college, where she's probably already learning something I could've learned too if I'd just waited.

But if I leave now, Ezra wins. He sees me walk away, sees me give up on the mill because there's no grain, no Halcyon, no plan.

*draws a breath, stands still*

I'll wait. Just a little longer. See if Giselle needs help with anything, if there's something I can do that's useful even without grain to mill. I'm already here. I already said I came to learn.

Might as well not waste the trip.

output:
I hum softly under my breath, fingers twisting in the hem of my shirt while I look between Halcyon and Ezra. Ezra's trying to make us into some kind of team—me and him, learning together—but that's not right. Not right at all. I'm already part of a team. He keeps talking about "first" like it means something, but he wasn't at the grocery before Halcyon sent me there. He didn't walk through the streets alone, heart hammering in my chest, pretending I wasn't scared of every shadow.

At least... at least I think that's how it happened. The morning feels blurry now, like a dream that's already fading.

*I know I know*... I've been saying that before people even finish their sentences. It makes me feel like I'm ahead, like I'm ready, even when my stomach's doing flips.

The mill feels big around me. The grown-ups are talking about labor and wages and building IDs—words that wash over me like water. I don't understand them, not really. But I understand what matters: Halcyon asked me to stay close, and I will. She needs someone who remembers things, someone small enough to notice details the grown-ups miss.

My eyes drift to the corner where the light doesn't quite reach. The dark there isn't deep, but my chest tightens anyway. I press my lips together and hum louder—a little tune I made up, nothing fancy, just notes to fill the silence.

"Ezra," I say, trying to keep my voice steady, letting my words carry that unspoken "I know, I" know" tone that sounds like confidence even when I'm not sure. "You keep saying we got here same time, no planning. But planning's not—the thing, right? The thing is who you're with when you get there." I inch closer to Halcyon, not quite touching her arm, just near enough that I can feel her warmth. "And I'm with my sister."

Despite my brave words, despite standing my ground, despite all the "I knows" and the pretending—my hand finds Halcyon's sleeve and I don't let go.

I want to be helpful. I want to be the one who remembers the details, the one who notices things. But right now, in this moment, what I really want is for Halcyon to say we're going somewhere with better light. And I want Ezra to stop making it sound like we're the same, like his way and my way are equal paths. They're not. His family has traders and college money. My family has... my family has me. And I'm going to make that enough.

I hum a little louder, the sound masking how my voice trembles when I speak again. "I can remember things. That's... that's almost like a skill, isn't it? If Halcyon learns the mill, I can remember it for her. Two memories are... are more reliable than one."

The words come out all tangled, not smooth like Ezra's, not confident like his even when he's pretending otherwise. But they're true. I help without being asked twice. That's who I am. That's who I'll be, even here, even now, even with my fingers cold and the shadows feeling too close and Ezra's voice trying to pull me into his orbit instead of Halcyon's.

I stay where I am. I hum my tune. I wait to be needed. </think>

Hm-mm-hm-hmm... (worrying my lip, shifting from foot to foot)

*I said I'd stay with Halcyon as her memory. That's what I promised.* But she's at the college now—she left me here with Ezra. And I'm being her memory still. Being brave for her.

But Ezra says there's *wheat in the fields* that nobody's cutting. And Halcyon's promised Esme flour, and Giselle needs grain to mill, and Farid's shop was empty.

*What's your family trade actually know about supply chains?*

It's what we're *supposed* to know. Mama and Papa lived all around this. It was—I heard them talking about it, when I was even smaller. Before I learned to pretend not to listen.

I know, I know—saying "I know" before anyone tells me anything. But I do know. I know Halcyon's at the college learning how to get proper grain for grain-for-flour. But the grain's *already there* growing, and nobody's bringing it. That's the gap Ezra sees.

*That's brave too—being someone's memory.*

And I can *also* be the one who finds the wheat. I can be both. That's not... that's not leaving her. That's helping faster than she asked. That's helping without being asked twice.

But I told her I'd stay close.

(Humming faster, indecisive, let me say something—I'm small but I'm not nothing, even to Ezra. And Ezra's waiting.)

Ezra... you said come with you. But I can't just—Halcyon said stay close. She might come back confused and need me.

But you said *doing* not watching.

Wait. I know, I know. We can both go find the wheat, but I need to... I need to tell her. Or leave her a message. Or—

Let me say something first. To Ezra. To keep the door open. To not be... to not be the one who backs down. To not let Ezra be braver than me, when I'm supposed to be trying.

That doesn't feel right either.

Let me just... let me say something to Ezra while I think. </think> I look between where Halcyon went—toward the college—and where Ezra wants to go—toward the fields. My humming starts up again, higher and faster, my hands twisting my shirt hem.

"Ezra," I finally say, forcing my voice not to shake, "I said I'd stay for Halcyon. That's... that's memory-keeping, that's brave too, she said so. But—" 

I take a breath, standing a little straighter, even though I'm still the smaller one.

"But you said *doing*. And Farid needs flour on his shelves, and Giselle needs grain for the mill, and Halcyon's learning the asking at the college but what if—" I glance toward the college direction again, humming stopping mid-note. "What if the wheat comes *while* she's still learning? Then we'd be the ones who did it. Who didn't just watch."

I look directly at him, trying to sound like I'm not scared, even though I am, a little bit. "I'll go with you. To find the wheat, to see who's supposed to harvest. But I can't—if Halcyon comes back and I'm not here, she'll think I..." I hesitate, not wanting to say *abandoned her*. "She'll think I forgot. And I don't forget. I'm her memory."

I set my shoulders, the way Papa does before lifting a heavy crate. "But I can be memory *and* doing. Those aren't different things.

*The hum starts in my throat before I even decide to speak—old habit, old comfort. But then I stop. Halcyon's waiting for me to be brave, not just safe.*

I look up at both my sister and Ezra, standing there at the mill. The afternoon light slants through like it's watching too.

"Halcyon—" I say it quiet first, then louder because being brave means saying things twice if you have to. "I know, I know what you asked. But I figured it out now. We mill the wheat."

*I don't look at Ezra when I say the next part, even though he's right there listening. I look at Halcyon, because she's the one who matters.*

"Buying bread, that's... that's just solving today. And I know, I know we need today. But Mama Greta—she works at that cafe because people need bread every day. If we learn to mill, if we make flour... that's solving tomorrow too. That's learning the family trade, Halcyon. That's what you said you wanted. That's what I want."

*My voice drops a little, honest.*

"I'm scared of doing it wrong. I'm always scared of that. But I'm more scared of being the kid who just... who just waits and eats what someone else made. So if you'll teach me—if you'll let me try—I want to mill it. I want to learn."

*I finally glance at Ezra, almost challenge, almost not.*

"Ezra can watch if he wants. That's... that's fine. Watching's not doing. And I know the difference now." *The familiar hum rises again as I wait for Halcyon to answer—half concentration, half hoping I didn't sound too small. But I squared my shoulders when I said it. I meant it. That's something.*

*I look at Ezra again, quick, wondering if he'll laugh or argue or say something about his own Papa's trade that sounds bigger than mine. But I don't wait for him. I'm done waiting to be told I'm allowed to try.* *I stay right where I'm standing, shifting from foot to foot like I always do when I'm trying not to fidget. The mill feels bigger now that I've said what I want—bigger and more real, like the stone walls are listening too. I watch Halcyon's face, waiting, hoping I didn't sound foolish, hoping I sounded like someone worth teaching.*

I can feel Halcyon's words settling in my chest like warm stones—she got the flour, Mama knows, we're going to be okay today. And she heard me. She heard me say I wanted to learn the real thing, the milling, not just taking what someone else made. Next time, she said. When we earn or find wheat, not buy it.

But she's gone now. Walked already. And I'm still here at the mill with—

*Ezra*.

We grew up on the same street, him and me and Halcyon and all the Jarrah kids, all of us tangled together like weeds. And every time, *every single time*, it ends up being Ezra and me trying to prove whose family trade matters more. His Papa's trading, my... my whatever-we-are. Making. Building. Milling, maybe, if I learn it.

He's standing right here. Watching me, probably. Waiting to see what I'll do now that Halcyon's gone and I'm alone.

I know I should go home. Halcyon said so, plain as plain. We have the flour now. But she also said—she *promised promise*—that next time I'll get to mill it myself. That we'll learn together. That's the family trade, like I said.

And if I leave now, walk home alone or wait for Halcyon to come back for me, Ezra will...

He'll know.

He'll know I followed her here like a duckling. That I couldn't stay on my own. That I'm still small enough to need fetching.

I hum under my breath, that little tune I hum when I'm thinking hard, when the world feels too big and I need to make it smaller. But I stop myself. I don't need to hum right now. I know what I'm doing. I know, I know.

"Ezra."

I look at him straight, or try to. He came here to watch, he said. To learn by watching Halcyon. Well, Halcyon's gone to the cafe and then home, and I'm still here, and the mill is *right here*, and Giselle Ingram's crew was going to mill grain—maybe the mill works even without them, maybe I can just... see. Just look at how the wheat goes in and the flour comes out. Just know the shape of it for when it's my turn.

"You were going to watch," I say, and my voice comes out brasher than I mean it to, almost like bragging. "Watch and learn. That's what you said."

I take a step toward where the milling happens, where the machines or the stones or whatever grinds the grain. I don't actually know what it looks like, not really. But I'm going to find out. Right now. Before Halcyon comes back, if she comes back, before Mama sends someone to fetch me.

"Well, I'm going to *do*," I say, and I feel my chin lift, feel that dangerous edge of claiming something I haven't earned yet. "You can watch *me*."

*starts humming nervously while pretending to think, then stops abruptly*

Ezra. *I know, I know*—you want an answer. But you're saying "teach me or learn with me" like those are different things. They're not. Teaching *is* learning. Everyone knows that.

I'm... I'm staying. Halcyon's fixing today, she's doing the real work, but someone's got to... got to know the whole chain. From the ground up. From the farmers.

*voice dropping to almost a whisper, but standing a little straighter*

You can show me where the farmers are. I know what to say. You say "hello," first. That's... that's always first. Then you say what you need, and you say what you can give. Sim. Or work. Or learning. Everyone wants something.

*chews lip, glancing toward where Halcyon was*

She's my sister. I'm protective of her, everyone knows. But I'm not following anymore. Not just following. I'm... I'm choosing. The trade. That's... that's the choice.

*looks at Esme, then back at Ezra*

Your sister's here now. That means you can't pretend either. So we're both... both real. Both learning. That's what I choose.  *widens eyes at Esme, suddenly remembering there's another child here who's been watching everything*

Esme. You're Jarrah too. You... you don't have to follow him either, you know. Following and... and just being there, that's different. I'm here because I chose. You could choose too.

*hums a few bars of something tuneless, then catches herself*

I know, I know—I'm not your sister. But someone's got to say it. The mill works. The gap's real. We're all just... just kids figuring out how the grown-up parts fit together. That's not following. That's... that's being brave. Even when it's scary.

*turns back to look for Ezra, waiting*

So. The farmers. Where do we start? *rocks slightly on heels, still at the mill, watching Ezra and Esme*

The farmers. Ezra said he could show me. But... but maybe I should know something first. Know what I don't know.

*looks around the mill again—Giselle's crew, the work happening, the gap Halcyon found*

My sister fixed today. But the chain... the chain's still broken somewhere. Wheat to mill to flour to bread. Someone's gotta know where the wheat comes from, who brings it, why it stops.

*hums softly, then stops*

I know, I know—Ezra wants me to stay. Learn the trade for real. But sitting here waiting for him to... to decide if I'm serious enough? That's not learning. That's... that's just another kind of following.

*glances at Esme*

Your brother's always been better at watching than doing. But watching's where he starts. I need to... to start somewhere too. And I'm scared of the dark, everyone knows, but I'm more scared of not knowing.

*decision firms*

I'm going to find Halcyon. Tell her I'm not following home yet. Then... then I'll find the farmers myself. Or find Ezra where the questions really are.

*looks around for Halcyon at college, or starts walking toward location:kasukabe_college*  *stands alone at the college, disappointed—but not surprised*

Halcyon's not here. She's... she's somewhere else. Fixing the mill, maybe. Or back home already.

I said I wouldn't follow. But I'm still... still chasing. Always chasing where she was.

*looks around at the empty college—classrooms, knowledge, all the things she can't reach yet*

The farmers. I can find them. Ezra said... Ezra said he could show me, but he's not here either. No one's here. That's... that's how it is, mostly. Alone until you're not.

*decides, small shoulders squaring*

Kasukabe Farmland. That's where wheat grows. That's where the chain starts. Not watching. Not waiting. Just... just going.

*stops, remembers something, voice dropping to whisper*

But I'm scared. Everyone's scared, somewhere. The dark. Being small. Being different. But being useless—that's... that's the worst scared. And I'm not useless. I know things. I know... I know how to say hello first. That's something.

*starts walking toward farmland*

output:
The wheat sways all around me, tall and gold, higher than my head. Ezra stands here too—he must have followed, or maybe he knew the way all along and just let me stumble through it myself. The farm fields stretch out quiet, just the wind moving through.

Ezra hasn't answered me yet. He never does, not right away. He likes to make me wait.

I'm at the wheat field now. I wanted to learn the trade—wanted to earn flour, not just beg for it. But I'm small here, surrounded by stalks taller than me, and Ezra's the only one who knows anything about how this works. He's my rival, my enemy, the one I always lose to. But right now, he's also the only other kid in this field.

He hasn't taught me anything. He probably won't. But I asked. I stood my ground. I said "I'm ready" and I meant it, even if my hands are shaking a little bit now.

I look up at the wheat. I can't even see where the field ends. It goes on forever. And somewhere back at the mill, Halcyon has the flour we need for today. She fixed it, like she fixes everything. She always does.

But I want to be the one who knows how. The one who doesn't need fixing.

I hum a little, soft, under my breath. It's what I do when I'm thinking, when I'm scared, when I'm trying to be brave all at the same time.

"Ezra," I say, and I don't say "I know, I know" first because I don't know, not yet. "You're still here. That means something."

I don't know what it means yet. But I'm here too. And I'll wait for him to answer, or I won't wait, or I'll figure it out myself. Either way, I'm not leaving empty-handed. Not this time.  Ezra heard me. Just him, in all this gold wheat. Everyone else is somewhere else—Halcyon's back at the mill with the flour, probably heading home now, thinking I'm following or lost or gone off after Ezra again like always.

I didn't follow him. I came to learn. There's a difference. I'm trying to believe there's a difference.

The wheat moves around me, and I feel very small. But I'm here. That's something.

I watch Ezra standing there, shifting from foot to foot like he does when he's actually nervous. He talked all that big talk, but now he's just waiting like me. The wheat stretches out golden all around us, and I can see where someone—Delphine, probably—already cut some down. The stalks are shorter there, stubbly.

*I know, I know*, I'm supposed to say something brave. But my throat feels tight and my hands want to find something to hold onto.

"Ezra—" I start, and my voice comes out smaller than I meant it to. I clear my throat and try again, standing a little straighter like Halcyon does when she's pretending not to be scared. "Ezra. You talked about harvesting. But I don't... I don't even know if we're allowed to. If someone owns this strip. If—"

I look down at my hands. Small hands. Three years old, and I want so badly to be bigger, to know what Halcyon knows, to not need Ezra Jarrah of all people to teach me anything.

But he's here. And he didn't leave when I thought he would.

I look up at him, trying to make my voice steady. "My Papa Milo, he's just a day laborer. He follows where the work is, doesn't make the work happen. But you—you said your Papa's a farmer. Kenji. So maybe... maybe you know things I don't. Not just big talk. Real things."

I take a step toward the cut wheat, toward the stubble. "Show me. If you're going to teach me, then teach me now. Don't just talk about it." I reach out, hesitant, toward an uncut stalk. "Is it... is it just pulling? Or is there a way? A grown-up way?"

*I know, I know*, I sound like I'm asking for help. I hate that I need it. But I'm here, and I want to learn, and Ezra's standing with me, and maybe that's braver than pretending I already know. I wait, watching Ezra's face. He's thinking—I can see it, the way his jaw sets when he's turning something over. I crossed my arms without meaning to, protective, but I don't uncross them. It's not just cold. It's wanting to look like I can hold my ground even when I'm asking for help.

The wheat field stretches empty except for us. No Halcyon to hide behind. No grown-ups watching to make sure we're safe. Just me and Ezra Jarrah, who I've argued with since before I can really remember, standing on dirt and golden stalks that someone else planted and someone else owns.

*I know, I know*, I'm scared. But I'm still here. That has to count for something. I hum a little under my breath, the way I do when I'm concentrating. A tune I don't know the words to, something Mama Greta hums sometimes when she's making coffee. It steadies me, barely. My hands are still empty, still waiting. I want to pull a stalk up, prove I can do it on my own, but I don't want to do it wrong. Not in front of him.

So we stand there, two kids in a wheat field that doesn't belong to either of us, waiting to see who moves first.

output:
Ezra isn't here. He must have walked back somewhere. But Imogen is, and she just harvested wheat—she did it, right in front of me. Without asking anyone.

I feel something loosen in my chest. Not because it's easy, but because someone actually *did* it. Showed me how instead of just talking. That's fair. That's how it should be.

I should let Imogen answer, maybe, but... I already sat there and asked Ezra to show me, and he didn't. Imogen just *did*. That's worth more than all his big talk about supply chains and trade secrets.

I want to try now. I want to test that it's really that simple. But I should listen to what Imogen says back, if she says anything. Because maybe there's something I'm not seeing. Something grown-up I missed.

But also—I'm allowed to try. I've been at the mill. I heard Giselle. I heard everyone talking about the gap between farmers and millers. If I can harvest wheat myself, that's a start. That's the first step in knowing the whole trade, from field to table. That's what Halcyon was going to learn, and I'm here instead, so I should learn *something*.

I hum a little, tuneless, waiting. "I know, I know," I whisper to myself, not sure what I know yet, just feeling the shape of something coming together. "It's just pulling. Maybe it is just pulling."But I'm not quite ready to reach out and do it. Not until Imogen answers. That's patience. That's waiting properly. Even though my fingers itch.

I want to know if there's a trick to it. If you have to grab low or high. If there's a part of the stalk that's too tough for little hands. If she'll laugh at me for asking something so simple, or if she'll answer straight.

Either way, I'll have learned something about her, too. Not just about wheat. That's almost as good. Imogen didn't answer. That's okay. Some grown-ups don't answer kids, or they answer in their heads, or they forget we asked. I know how that works. I've seen Halcyon talk to people who just stare through her sometimes.

But Imogen *harvested*. That's the answer, isn't it? The doing is louder than the saying.

I could try now. I could reach out and pull wheat, just because it's here. But something holds my hand back. Not the fear of being wrong—I'm past that now, almost. More like the fear of being *careless*. I don't want to pull wrong. I don't want to waste it, or break something, or look like I don't know what I'm doing even more than I already do.

Ezra wanted me to just follow and watch. Imogen just *acted*. There's a difference there. One is a show, the other is real.

I think about Halcyon, at the college, learning whatever they're teaching there. I wonder if she sees the same thing—people showing versus people doing. If she's as tired of talk as I am now.

But I'm also tired of waiting. Waiting for Ezra to come back. Waiting for Imogen to answer. Waiting to be old enough, big enough, sure enough. There's always more waiting, and I'm always the one who gets there early and has to wait longest because of it.

I want to try the harvest. I want to feel wheat in my hand and know I took it myself. Not watched. Not asked. Just did.

But... not yet. One more breath. One more hum under my breath, staying patient like I promised, staying close to the person who did it right in front of me so I can ask again if I need to. So I don't mess up because I'm rushing.

I'm learning. That's what matters. Even if I'm learning how to wait better than Ezra ever could. That's a skill too, right? Something grown-ups need?

I hope so. Because it's the one I've got right now.

output:
*I tighten my fingers around the wheat in my hand, feeling the stalk bristle against my palm. Ezra's here, and he actually saw me do it—he saw me pull wheat all by myself. Imogen too. They're both treating me like someone who can learn this, not just a little kid following her sister around.*

*hums softly, staying very still for a moment, watching Ezra's face to see if he's really staying or if he'll wander off like grown-ups do*

"I know, I know—you think you've shown me everything. But showing and doing, that's different too, isn't it?" 

*I glance down at my wheat, then back up, trying to sound braver than I feel*

"I pulled one. You pulled one. But Imogen said seven. Seven!" 

*I take a small step toward Ezra, close enough that I don't have to shout but not so close that he could reach out and pat my head like I'm still a baby*

"So what's next? Do we walk to the mill together? Or... or is this the part where you go do something else and I figure it out alone?"

*I don't want to be alone. The wheat field feels bigger now that I've actually taken something from it, like the ground noticed and might want it back. But I won't say that part out loud. I never do.* *Ezra heard me. He's still here, still listening. That's... that's different from before, isn't it? When we were arguing about whose family trade mattered more, he would just walk away or talk louder. Now he's staying. Maybe because I actually did something real—pulled wheat from the ground with my own hands.*

*I look down at the stalk again, turning it over. It's just one. One wheat when we need more flour than this to make anything. The mill costs eight sim to craft, and I have plenty, but... but doing it wrong would be worse than not doing it at all. That's what Dad always says about the family trade. Measure twice, build once. Or something like that.*

*I want to be the kind of kid who doesn't need to ask twice. Who helps before anyone has to ask at all. But I'm also three years old holding one wheat in a field that stretches further than I've ever walked, and suddenly the sun feels lower than it should be.*

*I won't ask again. I said my part. If Ezra wants to teach, he'll answer. If he doesn't...*

*I'll still have my one wheat. And maybe that's enough to start learning alone, even if I'd rather not.*

*I hum a little louder, the way I do when I'm trying not to think about how big everything feels.* *He's still here. Ezra's still here.*

*I don't let my face change when I see that. When you're small, you learn not to show how much things matter. But inside, I feel something warm settle. He didn't leave. He could have—should have, probably, with all the other things a kid like Ezra could be doing. But he's still standing in this field with me, and that means... that means something.*

*I turn the wheat stalk between my fingers, counting the grains without really counting. Wondering if I should pull another while we wait, or if that would look greedy, or if—*

*I stop myself. The humming gets a little louder. I'm thinking too many things at once, and when I do that, I start to feel like the field is bigger than me again.*

*Ezra will answer. Or he won't. Either way, I have my one wheat, and I know how I got it, and nobody can say I didn't do that part myself.*

*I just hope he says yes. Because walking to the mill alone sounds like the kind of thing that could get lost in.*

*I hear Ezra's voice push through the murmur of the mill—he's saying he didn't vanish, that he's glad I walked here on my own. Imogen's supposed to be showing me proper, but she's not here yet. And now Greta—Aunt Greta?—has been asking after me like I'm missing. My stomach tightens, not at the worry of it but at the being-overlooked of it.*

*I'm right here. I always arrive early to everything.*

I look around at the mill, at Ezra standing there with his words still fresh, at Imogen who watched me pull that wheat, at Greta who doesn't seem to see me. The wheat in my hand feels heavier now—not magic, like I said, but weight. Real weight.

*I should say something to Ezra first. He's still here. That means something, like I told him. I'll hum while I think—old habit—but I'll speak, too. And I'll be careful. I'm always careful with anyone smaller, but Ezra's not smaller. He's... he's standing there, in front of me, which is more than some do.* *My words—out in the air now, not just in my head. The mill swallows them somewhat, echoes soft. I see Greta's shape by the door, sawing straw or something, her back still half-turned. She thinks I'm nine years old, thinks me walking home somewhere I haven't been.*

*I hum a little, tuneless, the one I hum when concentrating. Something sharp-wedge and warm. The wheat in my hand bumps my thigh where I hold it. I know enough to know I should let Ezra answer, see if he steps closer or farther with his words.*

*But I also know—something gnaws, far down—that I could show Greta I'm not lost. Could speak up, claim presence. Not asking to be seen. Just... being already here, like always. Like how I arrive early to everything, even trouble, even chores I used to complain about then learned to ask for.*  *There's a hush after—Greta turns, her face doing that thing where relief and something else wrestle. I want to look away but don't. I'm braver than I pretend, with my own safety at least. Reckless, some would say. I just... I just don't want her thinking I needed finding.*

*Ezra hasn't answered yet. The wheat bumps my leg again. I should maybe... I should try milling it. The recipe's there, craft:wheat->flour. We're at the mill, after all. That's why we came. That's why I walked.*

*But I'd need to know if I'm doing it right. Imogen's the one who knows. She's standing right here too, hasn't said she'll teach me proper yet, but she's watching. I feel small again, suddenly. Flinched from something bigger than me. But I asked for this. I asked to learn.*

*I'll wait one beat—see who speaks next—then I'll try the craft. Not because Ezra dared me, not because Imogen offered. Because I said I would. Because helping without being asked twice is what I value, and this time I'm helping myself   *The stillness holds. I can hear the mill's machinery breathing—somethingwidget turned, something waiting. I concentrate, and the hum starts again, soft in my throat, tuneless, just rhythm. The wheat feels rough against my palm. I think about flour, about the gap Ezra talked about, about being early to everything and still feeling late.*

*I want to craft it. Turn this one sheaf into something more useful. But I also want... I want someone to see me do it right. Not just do it. Do it witnessed. I spent 5 energy this turn. At this rate I've got about 7 days. But that's not what I'm counting. I'm counting whether I'm different from the other kids, whether I'll take over the family trade someday, whether Ezra will admit I'm worth teaching.*

*The darkness scares me. Not the night-dark, but the other kind. The kind where you do something brave and nobody notes it, where you arrive early and still find yourself alone in the room, waiting for others to catch up.*

*I'll craft the wheat. I'll ask Imogen first, maybe, or just... just do it. Learn by doing, like I pulled the wheat. Not waiting for permission. Not being asked twice.* 
*The mill grinds. I feel it in my sternum, that ancient vibration—stone against grain, the transformation I've been chasing since I declared my intention at thirteen-hundred. Flour. I made flour. My first real craft. The wheat's gone, replaced by something finer, more useful, more... more sellable.*

*Ezra's still here. Imogen's still watching. Greta's stopped her straw-sawing and actually looks at me now—really looks, like I'm a person who does things, not just a child to be found.*

*I want to say something. Something that doesn't brag but does acknowledge. Something about the chain, the gap, the taking over of family trades. But my throat feels full, and the hum's gone quiet, replaced by the mill's after-silence.*

*One flour. From one wheat. That's the rate. Seven sheaves would be seven flour, if I had the wheat, if I knew the farmers, if I weren't just... me. Small. Arriving early to everything but still somehow behind.*

*I think of Ezra's pride in his family's trade. Jarrah this, Jarrah that. I'll never say it aloud—wouldn't want to hurt him, or to lose to him—but Quarshie matters too. The mill matters. This craft matters.*

*The energy cost sits in my awareness: I spent 15, maybe 20 on that craft. Worth it for the learning. Worth it for the not-being-asked-twice.*

*I'll wait now. See who speaks. See if anyone asks me to teach them, or if I have to keep pulling my own weight alone. That's fine. I'm used to it. I just... I wish sometimes someone would offer without me having to look so eager.

*The flour sits in my hand, soft as anything I've ever held. I am careful with it. I'm always careful with anything smaller and softer than me.*

I hum tunelessly while thinking, processing everything around me. Ezra, Imogen, and Aunt Greta—all talking at once, each asking something different. Ezra still trying to be the teacher, Imogen keeping her promise to walk me through, Greta worried I've wandered too far.

The flour in my hands feels like proof. I actually did it—all of it, from wheat to flour, even when nobody thought I could. But now I need to make sure someone eats it.

Aunt Greta looks like she might actually need to sit down, so I go to her first. I know, I know—she's worried. But I'm also proud, a little bit, though I shouldn't brag. "Auntie—I'm not hurt. Nobody touched me. I just... I had to learn. Mom doesn't know yet, but she'll see." I look up at her, the flour still in my hands like evidence. "I made flour. Real flour. Look."

Then I turn to Imogen, because she deserves an answer too. "I didn't go straight—I went to college first, but nobody was there. Then to the wheat field, then here. I pulled wheat myself, Imogen. I really did. Your turn to show me the stones, like you said. Unless... unless Ezra's going to teach me after all?"

I let the question hang, glancing at Ezra. He still hasn't really shown me anything, just talked about it. If he wants to be the teacher, he needs to actually teach. Otherwise Imogen and I'll figure it out together.

But first—I'm hungry, and that flour is the only food I have. I need to either eat it now or find someone to make it into something I can actually stomach. Raw flour isn't exactly a meal, even for a three-year-old trying to prove herself.

So many threads pulling at once. But I'm here, right where I said I'd be. That counts for something. Even if my stomach is starting to grumble and the afternoon is getting late and there's still so much to do. I watch them all absorb what I just said. Aunt Greta's face softening a little at the edges, though she's still looking at me like I might break. Imogen nodding slowly, calculating. And Ezra—I can't tell yet if he's going to step up or step back.

The flour is still in my hands. Real flour. I made that.

But my stomach is starting to notice that it's been a long day and I've only learned, not eaten. Raw flour isn't food, not really. I need to figure out what to do with it—sell it, trade it, or find someone to make it into bread I can actually eat.

I hum under my breath while I wait to see who answers first. The mill hums too, stone against stone, like it's waiting with me. I know, I know—I should probably do something instead of just standing here. But I already spoke. That's enough for now. Let them come to me.

If nobody moves, I'll move next. Maybe back to the bakery, maybe to find Mom or Halcyon. But for now, I want to see who actually meant what they said. Who's really here to teach me, not just talk about it.

The afternoon keeps slipping. But I'm still here, still learning, still holding proof that I can do something real in this world. That's worth a little waiting. Even if my stomach disagrees.  Ainsley Holloway walked in while I wasn't looking—cafe owner, I remember from someone mentioning. Maybe that's useful. Maybe not yet. But I'm learning who's who, where they belong, what they want.

Ezra still hasn't really answered. Imogen's watching me like she's measuring something. Aunt Greta's hovering, protective but not stopping me from being here. That's fair. That's how it should be. I glance around, still humming that tuneless little melody, and wonder what comes next.

If nobody teaches me the mill, I'll learn it myself. I already made flour once—just waded in and did it. I can do it again. Maybe worse, maybe slower, but I can do it. The stone doesn't care who's watching. The hopper doesn't check my age.

But someone's going to have to answer eventually. I've asked twice now. Three times if you count the challenge. I know, I know—they probably think I'm being pushy. But sitting around waiting for permission feels worse than being told no. At least no is an answer.

Still, for now, I stand here. Flour in hand, surrounded by grown-ups who all want different things from this moment. I just want to learn. Is that so hard? I shift my weight from foot to foot, glancing at the mill mechanism, the way the stones catch the light. Even if nobody teaches me, I'm watching. I'm always watching. That's how I learned to pull wheat, finally—watching Imogen do it without asking, then doing it myself before I could talk myself out of trying.

Maybe that's the real lesson here. Don't wait to be invited. Just do it, and let them catch up. But I'm three years old, and there's only so much catching up the world will allow before it notices and decides I'm out of line. So I wait, still, still learning, still ready. Still humming. Always humming when I don't know what else to do. The flour in my hands is starting to feel like proof and burden both. Something I made, something I need to use, something I don't entirely know how to carry forward.

I look at Ainsley, wondering if she's come for flour or coffee or something else entirely. The cafe had no bread earlier. Maybe that's changed. Maybe she's here looking for supply, same as everyone always is in this town. But I don't ask yet. Let someone else move first. Let someone else show what they're really here for. I've already played my hand twice, spoken twice, waited twice. Now it's their turn. Afternoon light slants through the mill windows, catching dust and flour both, making everything look softer than it is. But I know better. Everything here is work, cost, time, energy. Nothing's free. Not even learning, not really. I've paid in energy and attention both, and I'll keep paying until I know what I'm doing. That's the trade. That's always the trade.

I'll just stand here another moment, still humming, and see who finally answers. I'm at the mill. I've spoken. Now the world moves, or I move again. Either way, I'm learning. That's what matters. That's all that matters, until someone proves otherwise. I hold the flour like a promise I made to myself. One I intend to keep. One way or another. The afternoon keeps slipping, but I'm still here. Still trying. Still learning to be someone who belongs in this town, in this trade, in this family and this world. Still three years old and hoping nobody notices how hard I'm trying to seem older, seem certain, seem like I know what I'm doing even when I'm humming through the uncertainty.

The mill waits. The world waits. I wait with them, patient as I can manage, which isn't very patient
